lessons.title: Online Tutoring Basics
objectives: Tell apart the two businesses inside this course - selling your time live, and selling a recorded product - and say which one suits your situation now
Plan around the three things that actually stop Kenyan tutors working: connection, power and data cost
Separate knowing a subject from being able to teach it, and name the teaching skills you will have to build
lessons.notes:
This course covers two different businesses that get talked about as one thing. They have different economics, different risks and different starting costs. Choosing between them is the first real decision.

LIVE TUTORING: YOU SELL TIME

You meet a student on a video call and teach. You are paid per hour or per lesson.

- Income starts quickly. A tutor approved on a platform can be paid in the first month.
- Income stops when you stop. No lesson, no money.
- There is a hard ceiling. There are only so many teaching hours in a week, and teaching is tiring in a way that admin is not.
- The fixed cost is small: a working connection, a device, a quiet corner.

RECORDED COURSES: YOU SELL A PRODUCT

You record lessons once and sell access many times.

- Income arrives much later. Writing, recording and publishing a small course is weeks of unpaid work.
- It keeps earning after the work is done, in principle.
- The honest distribution is brutal. Most courses on open marketplaces sell in single or low double figures and earn very little. A few earn well. The difference is almost never video quality; it is whether anybody was already listening to you.
- The fixed cost is still small, but the time cost is large and paid up front by you.

WHICH ONE FIRST

If you need income this term, start with live tutoring. If you already teach the same thing repeatedly to different people and are tired of repeating yourself, record it. Many people end up doing both, where the recorded course is what convinces a stranger to book a live lesson.

THE THREE THINGS THAT ACTUALLY STOP PEOPLE

These are not footnotes. They are the operational core of tutoring from Kenya, and ignoring them is why tutors lose contracts.

1. CONNECTION. A video lesson needs a connection that holds for the full hour, not one that averages well. Platforms track cancellations and technical failures, and your rating falls when a lesson drops. Test your actual connection at the time of day you plan to teach, not at 6am when the network is quiet.

2. POWER. Plan for an outage in the middle of a paid lesson, because it will happen. A charged laptop plus a charged phone as a hotspot is the minimum workable backup. Know in advance what you will say and do when it happens: a short message to the student from your phone beats silence.

3. DATA. A one-to-one video call costs roughly 300 to 600 MB an hour at ordinary quality, and more if both cameras are on at high resolution. Twenty lessons a month is several gigabytes. Price that into your rate, as lesson 5 shows, instead of discovering it at the end of the month.

Three practical mitigations: turn off your camera when you are sharing a screen and talking over it, use audio-only for revision sessions where nobody needs to see a face, and schedule heavy uploads for whatever your provider treats as off-peak.

A FOURTH PROBLEM: TIME ZONES

Kenya is on East Africa Time, UTC plus three. That is useful. European evenings, when working adults take lessons, fall in your evening too. North American evenings fall in your small hours. If you want American students, you are choosing to work nights; decide that deliberately rather than by accident, and put your real availability on your profile so nobody books a 2am lesson you will cancel.

KNOWING A SUBJECT IS NOT TEACHING IT

The commonest reason a knowledgeable tutor gets poor reviews is that they explain at their own level. Teaching is a separate skill, and these parts of it are learnable:

- DIAGNOSING. Find out what the student can already do before explaining anything. Ask them to attempt a problem and watch where they stop.
- SEQUENCING. Break a skill into steps small enough that each one succeeds. A student who fails three times in a row stops trying.
- CHECKING. Do not ask whether they understand; they will say yes. Ask them to do the next one themselves while you watch.
- SILENCE. After a question, wait. Most tutors answer their own questions within four seconds and teach the student nothing.
- NAMING THE GOAL. Start each lesson by saying what the student will be able to do by the end, and finish by checking it.

If you do only one of these, do the checking. It is the difference between a student who books again and one who quietly disappears.

WHO YOUR STUDENT ACTUALLY IS

Three distinct markets, with different expectations:

- KENYAN SCHOOL STUDENTS AND THEIR PARENTS. The parent pays and wants evidence of progress against the syllabus and exams. Pays in shillings, often via M-Pesa. Expects you to know the curriculum.
- KENYAN ADULTS LEARNING A SKILL. Pays for a specific outcome, is time-poor, and will stop the moment lessons feel like school.
- INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS ON A PLATFORM. Usually language or exam preparation. Pays in dollars, minus platform commission and payment fees, and judges you against tutors worldwide.

Pick one to start. The profile, the price and the proof are different for each, and a profile written for all three convinces nobody.

TEACHING CHILDREN BRINGS OBLIGATIONS

If your students are under eighteen, you are not simply a freelancer. A parent or guardian must agree to the lessons and know when they happen. Say clearly whether lessons are recorded and who can see the recording, and get written permission before recording a child. Keep as little personal information about a child as you can, keep it somewhere private, and never post a student's work or face publicly without the parent's explicit permission. Children's personal data is treated as sensitive under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019; confirm the current requirements with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner rather than assuming you are exempt because you are one person.
lessons.practice:
Decide which business you are starting, then prove you can actually run a lesson.

Step 1. Write one sentence naming your choice: live tutoring, a recorded course, or live tutoring first with a course later. Write the reason in one more sentence, referring to how soon you need income.

Step 2. Write your student in one line: which of the three markets, what they want to be able to do, and who pays.

Step 3. Run a real connection test at the hour you plan to teach. Open a video call with a friend and stay on it for a full thirty minutes, sharing your screen for part of it. Record:

- Did the call hold for thirty minutes without dropping?
- How much data did it use? Check before and after on your device.
- Projected data cost for twenty one-hour lessons a month: ____

Step 4. Write your outage plan in three lines: what device is your backup, what is your backup connection, and the exact message you will send a student when power goes during a lesson. Save that message somewhere you can copy it in ten seconds.

Step 5. Set your real availability. Write the days and hours you would genuinely teach, in East Africa Time, and then write what those hours are for your intended student's time zone. If the overlap is tiny, say so now rather than after you have built a profile.

Step 6. Practise the teaching skill that matters most. Take one thing you know well and teach it to somebody for ten minutes. Rules: ask them to attempt something before you explain, and finish by having them do one themselves while you stay quiet. Afterwards write down where they got stuck and whether you waited or filled the silence.

If you will teach anybody under eighteen, add one line: how you will get the parent's written permission, and what you will tell them about recording.

quiz.question: You need income within the next month. Which is the honest choice?
options: Record a course, because it earns while you sleep
Live tutoring, because a recorded course is weeks of unpaid work before any income
Both at once, to double your chances
Neither is possible from Kenya

quiz.question: You plan to teach twenty one-hour video lessons a month. What should you do about data before setting your rate?
options: Nothing - data is a personal expense, not a business one
Assume lessons are cheap because messaging is cheap
Measure your actual usage on a test call, project the monthly cost, and build it into your rate
Switch to 4K video so the student sees you clearly

lessons.title: Recording Your First Lesson
objectives: Fix audio before touching video, because bad sound is what makes people stop watching
Record a short, single-idea lesson using a phone or laptop and free software, with settings that keep the file small enough to upload
Plan a lesson before recording it so you stop re-recording, which is where beginners lose most of their time
lessons.notes:
Most first recordings fail for reasons that have nothing to do with teaching. They fail because the sound echoes, because the file is too big to upload, or because the recording covered four ideas and ran thirty-five minutes.

AUDIO FIRST. IT IS NOT CLOSE

Viewers forgive a soft, grainy picture. They stop watching bad sound within seconds. Everything below costs nothing:

- RECORD IN A SOFT ROOM. Curtains, a bed, a sofa, clothes on hangers all absorb echo. A bare room with tile or concrete and a high ceiling is the worst case. If you only have a hard room, record sitting on the floor beside the bed, or drape a blanket behind you.
- GET THE MICROPHONE CLOSE. A phone held or clipped at about a hand's span from your mouth beats a laptop microphone a metre away, every time. Phone earphones with an inline microphone are better than either.
- KILL THE NOISE YOU CAN CONTROL. Switch off the fan. Close the window facing the road. Put your phone on silent, not vibrate, because vibration travels through the desk.
- WAIT FOR QUIET. Early morning and late evening are usually the quietest. Rain on an iron roof ends a recording session; accept that and reschedule.
- TEST BY LISTENING BACK, ON EARPHONES, BEFORE THE REAL TAKE. Thirty seconds of test audio saves an hour of wasted recording.

ONE IDEA, FIVE TO TEN MINUTES

A recorded lesson is not a class. Each video should teach one thing and then stop.

- One idea per video makes it findable, re-watchable and far easier to re-record when something changes.
- Five to ten minutes is the workable range for most topics. Over about fifteen, attention and data cost both bite.
- Your learner may be watching on a phone on a daily bundle. A short video they can finish is worth more than a thorough one they abandon at minute four.

A reliable structure for each video:

1. Say what they will be able to do at the end. One sentence.
2. Show it done, as a whole, quickly.
3. Walk through it slowly, in steps.
4. Name the mistake people usually make here.
5. Give them something to do before the next video.

PLAN, OR YOU WILL RE-RECORD FOREVER

Re-recording is the hidden cost of making a course. Two things prevent most of it.

An OUTLINE, not a script. A script read aloud sounds dead, and you will stumble over your own written sentences. Write instead a list of five to eight bullet points on one page, in order, large enough to read at a glance. You talk; the bullets keep you on the road.

A PRACTICE RUN. Say the whole thing through once without recording. You will discover the two places where you do not actually know what you think you know. Fix those, then record.

And when you fumble a sentence mid-take, do not start the whole video again. Pause, be silent for two seconds, and say the sentence again properly. You cut the bad one out later, and the silence makes it easy to find.

SCREEN LESSONS VERSUS TALKING TO CAMERA

If you are teaching anything on a computer, record the screen. Nobody needs to watch your face while you explain a spreadsheet, and a screen recording is far easier to make well.

- OBS Studio is free, works on Windows, Mac and Linux, and records screen plus microphone.
- Most phones and both major desktop systems also have a built-in screen recorder, which is enough to start.
- Clean the screen before you record: close other tabs, hide personal notifications, zoom the text up so it is readable on a phone, and turn off anything that pops up.

If you do appear on camera, face a window rather than having it behind you, and put the phone at eye level on a stack of books instead of pointing up at the ceiling.

SETTINGS THAT KEEP THE FILE UPLOADABLE

This is where Kenyan bandwidth decides your workflow.

- RECORD AT 1080p, NOT 4K. On a phone screen the difference is invisible and the file is several times larger. For screen recordings, 1080p at 30 frames a second is plenty.
- EXPECT ROUGHLY 60 TO 150 MB for a well-compressed ten-minute 1080p video, and much more straight out of a phone camera. Check the actual file size before you plan an upload.
- UPLOAD WHEN THE NETWORK IS QUIET, usually late at night, and upload one video at a time. A failed upload at 80 percent costs the whole file's data.
- KEEP THE ORIGINALS on the device and on one other place. Re-recording a lost lesson is far more expensive than storage.

EDITING: DO THE LEAST THAT WORKS

Your first course does not need transitions, music or a logo animation. It needs the dead parts removed.

- Cut the start before you begin speaking and the end after you finish.
- Cut the fumbles you marked with silence.
- Stop there. Free editors such as the ones built into most phones, or a free desktop editor, are enough for that.

Add captions if the tool makes it easy. Many learners watch without sound, in a crowded place, or are not confident in English, and captions help all three.

WHEN SOMETHING IS WORTH TEACHING WITHOUT VIDEO

Some things are better written than recorded: a list of commands, a checklist, the exact syllabus topics covered. Put those in the written notes beside the video rather than reading them aloud. A learner can copy from text; they cannot copy from your mouth at speed.
lessons.practice:
Record one five-minute lesson, end to end, and check the file is actually usable.

Step 1. Pick one thing you can teach in five minutes. One thing. If your topic needs ten minutes, it is two videos.

Step 2. Write the outline on one page: the sentence saying what the learner will be able to do, then five to eight bullets, then the mistake people usually make, then the task you will set them.

Step 3. Prepare the room. Note which surfaces will absorb echo, switch off the fan, silence your phone, and choose the quietest hour you have.

Step 4. Record thirty seconds of test audio, listen back on earphones, and write down what you heard: echo, hum, traffic, roof noise. Fix the worst one before continuing.

Step 5. Say the whole lesson aloud once without recording. Write down the two places where you hesitated, and settle them.

Step 6. Record the real take. When you fumble, pause for two seconds and say the sentence again. Do not restart.

Step 7. Check the result and write these numbers down:

- Length: ____
- File size: ____ MB
- Resolution you recorded at: ____
- Time to upload it at your usual connection: ____

If the file is over about 200 MB for five minutes, you recorded at too high a setting. Change it and note the new setting.

Step 8. Do the minimum edit: trim the start and end, cut the fumbles. Then watch the whole thing back on a phone, at phone volume, and write one sentence on the single thing you would change next time.

quiz.question: You have time to fix exactly one thing about your first recording. Which should it be?
options: Camera resolution, from 1080p to 4K
The audio - echo, microphone distance and background noise
Adding an intro animation and background music
Buying a ring light

quiz.question: You fumble a sentence six minutes into a ten-minute take. What is the right move?
options: Start the whole video again from the beginning
Carry on and hope nobody notices
Pause, stay silent for two seconds, say the sentence again properly, and cut the bad one later
Stop recording and switch to writing the lesson instead

lessons.title: Publishing a Course on Udemy
objectives: State what a marketplace actually gives you and what it takes, including how the revenue share changes depending on who brought the student
Meet the publishing requirements and plan a course that clears review the first time
Compare a marketplace against selling direct, and choose on the basis of whether you have an audience
lessons.notes:
A course marketplace is a shop that already has customers. That is the whole value, and it is a real one. What you give up in exchange is control over price and most of the revenue on sales the shop brings you.

Terms change, so read the current instructor agreement and revenue pages yourself before building a business on any figure. What follows is the shape of the deal and the parts that most surprise first-time instructors.

THE DEAL, PLAINLY

- WHO BROUGHT THE STUDENT DECIDES YOUR SHARE. When a student finds your course through the marketplace itself, the platform keeps the large majority of the sale. When you bring the student yourself, through your own link or coupon, you keep nearly all of it. The same course, the same student, can pay you several times more depending on which link they clicked.
- THE PLATFORM CONTROLS PRICING AND DISCOUNTS. Big marketplaces run near-permanent sales. You may set a list price, but your course will often sell at a fraction of it, and your share is a share of what the student actually paid, not of your list price.
- IT IS NOT EXCLUSIVE, BUT CHECK. Most marketplaces let you teach the same material elsewhere. Some promotional programmes add conditions. Read before enrolling in any extra programme.
- PAYMENT COMES WITH A LAG AND A METHOD. Expect a delay of weeks after the month closes, payment in dollars through a service such as PayPal or Payoneer, and a minimum balance. From Kenya, add currency conversion and withdrawal fees to your arithmetic.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE

If you have no audience, a marketplace can still sell your course, but at a low effective price and a small share. Earning a meaningful amount that way takes many sales, which takes a course that genuinely ranks well in a crowded category.

If you DO have an audience, the marketplace is the worst place to send them, because your own coupon link pays you several times more than their organic one. Use your audience on your own link, or sell direct.

That single fact decides most of the choice below.

CLEARING REVIEW THE FIRST TIME

Marketplaces have mechanical minimums, and courses get rejected for failing them rather than for being badly taught. Check the current requirements on the platform, but expect something like:

- A minimum total length of video, commonly around thirty minutes, and a minimum number of separate lectures, commonly five.
- Video at high definition, with a standard aspect ratio and no black bars.
- Audio that comes from both channels, is free of background noise and hiss, and is loud enough.
- A course image at the platform's exact dimensions, with no text that breaks their rules.
- A real curriculum: sections, a stated outcome, and no placeholder titles.

Two rejections that are easy to avoid: audio recorded on one channel only, so half of headphone users hear nothing, and a promotional video that is just you talking with no sense of what the course delivers.

WHAT MAKES A COURSE FOUND, NOT JUST PUBLISHED

Inside a marketplace, your competition is every other course in the category. Three things move the needle, and none is video polish:

- A TITLE THAT NAMES THE OUTCOME AND THE AUDIENCE. Not "Mastering Excel" but "Excel for bookkeepers: build a monthly report from raw sales data".
- A SPECIFIC NICHE. A general beginner course competes with thousands. A course on exactly the thing you know well, for exactly one kind of learner, competes with a handful. Narrow is an advantage here, not a limitation.
- EARLY HONEST REVIEWS. The first few reviews decide whether the platform shows your course to anyone. They have to be real; soliciting fake reviews gets courses removed.

THE ALTERNATIVE: SELLING DIRECT

Platforms that host and sell your course while you keep most of the money exist - the kind where you pay a monthly fee or a small transaction cut and do all the selling yourself.

- YOU KEEP FAR MORE PER SALE and you set the real price.
- YOU GET NO CUSTOMERS. Every single buyer comes from your own effort.
- YOU CAN SELL IN SHILLINGS and accept local payment, which matters enormously for Kenyan buyers. A dollar checkout loses most of a Kenyan audience.

A sensible sequence for many people: teach free on a channel or in a community until a few hundred people trust you, then sell direct at a real price in a currency your buyers hold. The marketplace route makes more sense when your subject has strong marketplace demand and you have nobody to sell to yet.

A HYBRID THAT WORKS

Put a smaller, introductory version on the marketplace, priced to be found. Use it to reach people who would never have heard of you, and inside it mention the deeper work you sell directly. Check the platform's rules on external links before you do this; most restrict promotion inside course content, and breaking that rule gets courses pulled.

BEFORE YOU SPEND SIX WEEKS RECORDING

Do this first, because it has saved people months. Search the marketplace for your intended course. Look at the top three results and write down: how many students they have, when they were last updated, what their reviews complain about. If the top courses are huge, recent and well reviewed, either find a narrower angle or choose the direct route where you compete on trust instead of ranking. The complaints in their reviews are a free specification for what your course should do differently.
lessons.practice:
Decide marketplace or direct on evidence, then prepare the thing that gets you accepted.

Step 1. Answer the deciding question in writing: how many people today would open a message from you about a course? Not followers - people who would actually open it. If the answer is under about fifty, the marketplace is the reasonable starting point. If it is in the hundreds, selling direct deserves serious weight.

Step 2. Research the competition properly. Search the marketplace for your topic and record, for each of the top three courses: student count, last update date, and the two commonest complaints in the reviews.

Step 3. From those complaints, write one sentence describing how your course will be different. This is your actual positioning, and it came from evidence rather than imagination.

Step 4. Write the title in the outcome-plus-audience shape. Then write the one-line promise: by the end of this course you will be able to ____.

Step 5. Build the curriculum on one page: sections, lecture titles, and the minutes you estimate for each. Add it up and check it clears the platform's minimum length and lecture count. Write both current requirements down from the platform page, not from this lesson.

Step 6. Work out your real earnings for one sale, both ways:

- List price: ____
- Likely actual sale price after platform discounts: ____
- Your share on a sale the platform brought: ____
- Your share on a sale you brought with your own link: ____
- After currency conversion and withdrawal fee: ____

Step 7. Write one sentence on where you will send anybody you personally tell about the course, and why.

Step 8. Check your existing recording against the technical requirements: resolution, aspect ratio, and whether your audio plays in both ears. Test the last one on earphones; it is the rejection people do not see coming.

quiz.question: You have a mailing list of 800 people who open your messages. Where should you send them to buy your course?
options: Through the marketplace's own search, so it counts as organic
Through your own coupon or direct link, because a sale you bring pays you several times more than one the platform brought
It makes no difference, the share is fixed
Nowhere - a list is for free content only

quiz.question: What is the honest trade-off of selling a course directly instead of on a big marketplace?
options: You keep far more per sale, but you must find every single buyer yourself
You keep more per sale and the platform still brings you customers
It is cheaper for the student but worse for you
Direct selling is not possible from Kenya

lessons.title: Becoming a Tutor on Preply
objectives: Build a tutoring profile that gets booked, treating the intro video and the first paragraph as the parts that decide
Work out your real hourly earnings after platform commission, payment fees and unpaid preparation time
Run a trial lesson that converts, and follow platform rules on student contact without giving up your ability to build your own practice
lessons.notes:
Tutoring marketplaces connect you to students worldwide and handle scheduling and payment. They take a commission and they own the relationship. Both halves matter.

Terms differ between platforms and change over time, so read the current tutor agreement yourself. What follows is the structure that is common across them and the parts that catch people out.

HOW THE COMMISSION USUALLY WORKS

On several major platforms the commission is not flat. It starts high on your first lessons with a new student - sometimes taking most or all of a first trial lesson - and falls as you accumulate taught hours with that student. The logic is that the platform paid to find them and recovers that cost early.

Two consequences follow, and they shape everything:

- A ONE-OFF STUDENT IS BARELY WORTH TEACHING. Most of that first lesson's money is commission. Your earnings come from students who stay.
- RETENTION IS THE WHOLE GAME. A student who books twenty lessons is worth many times a student who books one, even at the same rate. Everything in your teaching should be aimed at the student booking again.

WHAT YOUR LISTED RATE IS NOT

Your listed rate is not your earnings. Work through it honestly:

- Start with your hourly rate.
- Subtract the platform commission at your current tier.
- Subtract the payment service fee and the currency conversion loss when you move dollars to shillings.
- Now divide by the TOTAL time the lesson costs you: the hour itself, plus preparation, plus messages, plus the notes you send afterwards. For a well-taught lesson that is often ninety minutes or more of your time for sixty minutes of pay.
- Subtract the data the call consumed.

The number at the end is your real hourly earnings, and it is often half the figure on your profile. Lesson 5 turns this into a rate you can defend.

THE PROFILE: THREE PARTS DECIDE IT

Students scroll a list of tutors. Three things decide whether they stop at you.

THE INTRO VIDEO. This matters more than everything else combined, because it is the only evidence of what a lesson with you feels like. Keep it under two minutes. Say who you help and with what, in the first ten seconds. Then show, briefly, how you teach one small thing - actually teach it, do not describe your teaching philosophy. Speak to the camera as if to one person. Clear audio beats a nice background.

THE FIRST TWO LINES OF YOUR DESCRIPTION. Only these are visible before a student clicks. They must name the student and the outcome: who you teach, and what they will be able to do. Not your biography.

YOUR CREDIBILITY, STATED SPECIFICALLY. Certificates if you have them, but specifics beat credentials: the exam you prepare people for, the syllabus you know, the number of students you have taken through it. If you are starting, say what you have actually done rather than inflating it; students detect inflation and platforms remove it.

Two practical profile facts: your response time and your cancellation record are usually visible or feed the ranking, so answering messages quickly and never cancelling are part of getting booked, not just good manners. And put your genuine availability in your own time zone, as lesson 1 covered - a calendar you then cancel against is worse than a narrow one.

THE TRIAL LESSON: HOW IT IS WON

A trial is not a free sample of a normal lesson. It is a diagnosis plus a plan. Students rebook when they leave knowing what is wrong and what you will do about it.

Run it in this order:

1. Ask what they want to be able to do, and by when. Write it down in front of them.
2. Have them attempt something real, early, while you watch quietly. This is the diagnosis and most tutors skip it.
3. Teach ONE thing properly - the single most useful thing you noticed. Not a tour of everything they got wrong.
4. Have them do one themselves, successfully. They need to feel progress inside the trial.
5. Say out loud what you would work on over the next five lessons, in order.
6. Send a short written summary afterwards: what you saw, the plan, one thing to practise.

That last step costs you five minutes and is the commonest difference between tutors who fill their calendar and tutors who do not.

PLATFORM RULES ON TAKING STUDENTS OFF-PLATFORM

Platforms prohibit arranging paid lessons outside their system with students they introduced, and they enforce it - the usual penalty is removal and loss of pending earnings. The messaging is often monitored for contact details for this reason.

Do not do it. It is not worth your account, and the student who found you on a platform came to you because the platform was there.

What you CAN do, and should, is build your own practice in parallel from your own sources: your community, referrals from people you already know, your own channel, a local network. Students who find you directly are yours and carry no commission. Over time most successful tutors end up with a mixture, and the platform becomes the part they can turn up or down.

WHEN A PLATFORM IS THE WRONG FIT

Be honest about this. If you teach the Kenyan school curriculum to Kenyan students paid for by Kenyan parents in shillings, an international marketplace is a poor fit: its students want languages and international exams, its payment is in dollars, and its commission takes a share of a price Kenyan parents would not pay anyway. That market is reached through parent and school networks, which lesson 6 covers. Use the platform for what it is good at - international demand you could not reach yourself.
lessons.practice:
Build the profile pieces that decide bookings, and know your real rate before you publish one.

Step 1. Write the first two lines of your description. They must contain who you teach and what they will be able to do. Then delete every word about yourself that does not help a student decide.

Step 2. Script your intro video on one page, under two minutes spoken. Structure: who you help, in ten seconds; then actually teach one small useful thing; then one line on what a first lesson will look like. Record a test take and listen on earphones.

Step 3. Work out your real hourly earnings. Fill in every line:

- Listed rate per hour: ____
- Less platform commission at the starting tier: ____
- Less payment service and currency conversion: ____
- Total time the lesson really costs, including prep, messages and follow-up notes: ____ minutes
- Data cost for the call: ____
- REAL earnings per hour of your time: ____

Step 4. Write one sentence on whether that number is worth your time. If it is not, do not lower the rate - either shorten the unpaid work or reconsider the market. Lesson 5 deals with this properly.

Step 5. Plan your trial lesson as a sequence, in writing, using the six steps in the notes. Write the actual task you will ask a new student to attempt in step 2, and the written summary template you will send afterwards.

Step 6. Write your honest availability in East Africa Time, then convert it to the time zone of the students you want. Write the number of overlapping hours per week.

Step 7. Write one line each on two things you will do in parallel: how you will keep the platform's rules on student contact, and where your own non-platform students will come from.

quiz.question: On platforms where commission starts high and falls with accumulated hours, what follows for how you should teach?
options: Take as many one-off students as possible to build volume
Aim everything at the student rebooking, because earnings come from students who stay
Charge the highest possible rate on the trial lesson
Teach only trial lessons, since they are the easiest to fill

quiz.question: A student you met on a tutoring platform suggests paying you directly outside the platform to avoid its fees. What should you do?
options: Accept, since the fees are unfair to tutors
Accept but keep booking some lessons on the platform to stay unnoticed
Decline and keep lessons on the platform, because this breaches the agreement and usually costs you the account and pending earnings
Ask the platform for permission by message

lessons.title: Pricing Your Course or Tutoring
objectives: Build a price upward from your real costs, including commission, payment fees, data and unpaid working time, so you know your floor
Price against the value of the outcome rather than against the cheapest tutor in the list
Raise your rate using evidence, and structure packages without creating refund problems
lessons.notes:
Most tutors price by looking at what other people charge and going slightly lower. That is how you end up working more hours for less money than a salaried job, which is the commonest outcome in this field. Pricing has two honest inputs: what it costs you, and what the outcome is worth.

YOUR FLOOR: WHAT AN HOUR ACTUALLY COSTS YOU

Work this out once, properly, and keep the page.

Per lesson:

- Data for the call
- Share of your monthly connection cost
- Platform commission, at your current tier
- Payment service fee and currency conversion loss
- Wear on equipment: a laptop and a phone that need replacing every few years is a real monthly cost; divide it by the lessons you teach
- Your unpaid time: preparation, messages, scheduling, follow-up notes

That last line is the one people leave out, and it is usually the biggest. A lesson that takes thirty minutes of preparation and ten minutes of follow-up is a ninety-minute job, so an hourly rate of X is really two-thirds of X before any other cost.

Add it up and you have a floor. Below the floor you are paying to work. You are allowed to choose that briefly and deliberately - to gather your first reviews, say - but you must know you are doing it, and for how long.

THE SAME ARITHMETIC FOR A RECORDED COURSE

A course has no per-lesson cost but a large fixed one.

- Hours to plan, record and edit: be honest, including re-recording
- Multiply by what an hour of your time is worth
- That is the amount you must recover before the course has earned anything

Then: price, minus platform share, minus payment fees, equals your net per sale. Divide the fixed cost by that net and you have the number of sales at which the course breaks even. Write that number down. If it is in the thousands, the plan is wrong - either the price is too low or the course should be sold directly.

WHAT THE OUTCOME IS WORTH

The ceiling is not set by your costs. It is set by what the result is worth to the student.

- A student who passes an exam they would otherwise retake saves a year.
- A professional who finally builds their own monthly report saves hours every month, permanently.
- A parent whose child moves from failing to passing is not comparing you with other tutors; they are comparing you with the consequence.

So describe what you sell as the outcome, not as hours. "Six weeks to a working monthly report" can be priced as the thing it is. "An hour of Excel tutoring" is priced against every other hour of Excel tutoring in the world, which is a competition decided by whoever will accept least.

WHY BEING THE CHEAPEST FAILS

Three reasons, all observed repeatedly:

- Price signals quality when the buyer cannot judge skill in advance. The cheapest tutor in a list is often read as the least able.
- The cheapest tutor attracts the most demanding and least committed students, who cancel most and complain most.
- It leaves you nowhere to go. You cannot deliver more for less, so you deliver less, and the reviews follow.

If you need to win work without cutting your rate, change what is included rather than what it costs: a written lesson summary, a short practice set, a progress check every fourth lesson. Those cost you little and are worth a lot to a parent who wants evidence.

PRICING FOR DIFFERENT MARKETS

Charge what the market can actually pay, and do not confuse the two markets:

- KENYAN PARENTS AND STUDENTS pay in shillings from a household budget. Price in shillings, accept M-Pesa, and set the figure against local tutoring rates in your town rather than against international platforms.
- INTERNATIONAL PLATFORM STUDENTS pay in dollars against a worldwide field. Here your cost advantage is real, but so is the commission, and underpricing to the bottom of the field is a trap for the reasons above.

Running both at once is fine, and normal. Just keep the two price lists separate and never quote one in the other's context.

PACKAGES, CAREFULLY

Selling blocks of lessons is good for you: it improves commitment and reduces the admin of chasing single bookings. Two cautions:

- Say in writing, before payment, what happens to unused lessons, how much notice a cancellation needs, and whether the block expires. Ambiguity here produces the arguments that end tutoring relationships.
- Be fair and clear about refunds. Kenyan consumer protection law prohibits misleading representations, and a package whose terms were never explained is a dispute waiting to happen. A short, plain written policy protects you more than it costs you.

Also make sure the money reaches you cleanly: a prepaid block collected by M-Pesa is simple, while dollars through a platform carry commission and conversion. Compare the net, not the headline.

RAISING YOUR RATE

Raise it on evidence, not on frustration.

The evidence that justifies an increase: a full calendar, a waiting list, students who have stayed many months, results you can name - this many students through that exam, this proportion improving a grade.

How to do it: raise the rate for NEW students first and leave existing students on the old rate for a stated period, then tell them in advance, in writing, with a reason that refers to results rather than to your costs. Give them a clear date. Expect a few to leave; if nobody does, you raised it too little.

And raise it in meaningful steps. A five percent increase is not worth the conversation.

TAX IS NOT OPTIONAL

Tutoring income is income, whether it arrives as M-Pesa from a parent or as dollars from a platform. Keep a record from the first payment: date, student or platform, gross, fees, net, and the rate if it was converted. Which regime applies depends on your total turnover and registration, and those thresholds move - confirm your own position with KRA or an accountant rather than relying on any figure here. Build the eventual tax into your rate from the start; discovering it later is how a workable rate turns out not to have been one.
lessons.practice:
Work out your floor, then set a price you can defend out loud.

Step 1. Calculate your real cost per teaching hour. Fill in every line, in shillings:

- Data for one lesson: ____
- Share of monthly connection cost per lesson: ____
- Platform commission on one lesson: ____
- Payment and currency conversion: ____
- Equipment replacement, per lesson: ____
- Unpaid minutes per lesson - prep, messages, follow-up: ____
- Total cost, and total minutes of your time per paid hour: ____
- YOUR FLOOR per paid hour: ____

Step 2. Write your outcome sentence: by the end of working with me, a student will be able to ____, within ____ weeks. Price that, not the hour.

Step 3. Set two separate prices: one in shillings for local students paid by M-Pesa, one in dollars for a platform. For each, write the net you actually keep after all deductions. If either net is below your floor, write what you will change - not the rate, but what is included or which market you serve.

Step 4. If you are making a recorded course, calculate the break-even:

- Hours to produce it: ____
- Value of an hour of your time: ____
- Fixed cost: ____
- Net per sale after platform share and payment fees: ____
- SALES NEEDED TO BREAK EVEN: ____

Write one sentence on whether that number is realistic given the audience you have today.

Step 5. Write the three things you will include that cost you little and matter a lot: for example a written lesson summary, a practice set, a progress check every fourth lesson. These are what you offer instead of a discount.

Step 6. Draft your package terms in four plain lines: how many lessons, how long the block lasts, how much notice a cancellation needs, and what happens to unused lessons. Read it aloud and remove anything a parent could misread.

Step 7. Write your rate-raise rule now, while it is easy: the evidence you will require, the size of the increase, how much notice existing students get. Date the page.

Step 8. Start the income record: date, student or platform, gross, fees, net, currency and rate. Write one line naming what you will confirm with KRA about declaring this income.

quiz.question: You charge KSh 1,000 an hour. Each lesson also takes 30 minutes of preparation and 10 minutes of follow-up notes. Before any other cost, what are you actually earning per hour of your time?
options: KSh 1,000, since that is your rate
About KSh 600, because the lesson really occupies 100 minutes of your time
About KSh 1,400, because preparation adds value
It cannot be calculated

quiz.question: A new tutoring platform shows many tutors in your subject charging less than you. What is the sound response?
options: Undercut the cheapest one to get booked
Match the average exactly, to look normal
Hold your rate and compete on the outcome and on low-cost inclusions such as written summaries and progress checks
Leave the platform

lessons.title: Getting Your First Students
objectives: Get the first five students from people who already trust you, rather than from advertising to strangers
Build proof a stranger can check - a sample lesson, a named result, a real review - and ask for reviews in a way that gets them
Reach Kenyan parents and learners where they actually are, and handle minors safely and lawfully
lessons.notes:
The first five students are a completely different problem from the next fifty. The first five come from trust you already have. Advertising to strangers before you have any proof is the slowest possible route, and it is where most people start.

WHERE THE FIRST FIVE COME FROM

List the people who already know you can do this thing. Then ask them directly, naming the student you want.

- Former classmates, colleagues and juniors you helped informally
- Teachers at schools you attended, who get asked for tutor recommendations constantly
- Your church, mosque or community group, where parents talk to each other about exactly this
- Parents in your own neighbourhood, who trust proximity and a known face above everything
- WhatsApp groups you are genuinely part of - a parents' group, an estate group, a course group

The ask that works is specific. Not "let me know if you hear of anything". Instead: "I am teaching Form 2 maths online, two evenings a week, KSh X a session. If you know a parent whose child is struggling with it, please pass on my number." Specific asks get passed on because the person can picture who to pass it to.

Note what is happening here. A referral from somebody trusted skips every proof problem you have. That is why it is first, and why it keeps working long after you are established.

PROOF A STRANGER CAN CHECK

Beyond your circle, nobody takes your word for anything. Build three things:

A SAMPLE LESSON, PUBLIC. One five to ten minute recording, teaching one real thing, available to anybody. This is the single most useful asset you will make. It answers the only question a stranger has - what is a lesson with you like - and it works while you sleep. The recording skills from lesson 2 are exactly for this.

A NAMED RESULT, HONESTLY STATED. Not "I help students improve". Instead: "I took four students through Form 3 chemistry last year; three moved up a grade." If you have no results yet, say what you have actually done and do not inflate it. Fabricated results are both a consumer protection problem and the fastest way to lose the referral network that is your real asset.

REVIEWS, ASKED FOR PROPERLY. Most students never review unless asked, and a vague ask gets a vague review. Ask at the right moment - just after a visible success, not at the end of a long slog - and ask for something specific: "Would you write two lines about where you were when we started and what you can do now?" A review that names a starting point and an outcome persuades; "good tutor" does not. Never pay for a review or write one yourself.

WHERE KENYAN LEARNERS AND PARENTS ACTUALLY ARE

Be concrete about channels rather than posting everywhere:

- WHATSAPP is where parents organise and recommend. One genuine recommendation in a parents' group beats fifty posts to strangers. Earn it by being useful in the group first; broadcasting adverts into groups gets you removed, as the affiliate lesson on the same mistake explains.
- SCHOOL AND TEACHER NETWORKS. Teachers are asked for tutor recommendations constantly and are the highest-value contact you can make. Approach them respectfully, with a clear statement of what you teach and your availability, and never try to poach their classes.
- FACEBOOK GROUPS for parents, exam candidates, and specific skills. Read the rules; most ban direct advertising but allow helpful answers, and helpful answers are how people find you.
- YOUTUBE OR TIKTOK, if you will keep publishing. Short teaching clips are proof and reach at once. This is a slow build, not a launch tactic.
- YOUR PLATFORM PROFILE, for international students. There, ranking depends on response time, completed lessons and reviews, so the first students you do get matter more than any marketing.

For skills taught to adults, a free short workshop converts well: one hour, one genuinely useful thing taught properly, and at the end a clear statement of what the paid work is. It is proof and a sales conversation in one, and it costs you an hour.

THE HONEST LIMIT ON FREE WORK

Free lessons to build reviews can work, but set the boundary before you start: how many, for how long, and what you get in return - a review, a testimonial, a referral. Open-ended free tutoring does not convert into paid tutoring; it converts into a student who expects free tutoring. Write the limit down and keep it.

RETENTION IS CHEAPER THAN RECRUITMENT

Finding a student is far more work than keeping one. The things that keep them are small and unglamorous:

- Start on time, every time
- Begin each lesson by naming what they will be able to do by the end, and finish by checking it
- Send a short written summary afterwards: what we did, one thing to practise
- Tell the parent, unprompted, what changed this month
- Never cancel. If you must, give as much notice as you possibly can and offer a replacement slot immediately

That fourth point wins more work than any advertising. A parent who hears monthly that their child is progressing tells other parents.

TEACHING MINORS: DO THIS PROPERLY

If your students are under eighteen, this is not optional and it is not paperwork.

- A parent or guardian must agree to the lessons and know when they happen. Keep them informed.
- Say plainly whether lessons are recorded, who can see a recording, and how long you keep it. Get written permission before recording a child.
- Prefer an arrangement the parent can see: a shared calendar, a family device, a parent who can walk past. Avoid private channels between you and a child.
- Keep the minimum personal information, keep it somewhere private, and delete it when the lessons end.
- Never publish a child's face, name, work or results without the parent's explicit written permission - including in your own marketing, where the temptation is strongest.

Children's personal data is treated as sensitive under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019. Confirm the current obligations with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner rather than assuming a single tutor is exempt. Beyond the law, this is what makes parents recommend you, and parents recommending you is the whole business.
lessons.practice:
Get the first five students from trust, and build the one asset that works on strangers.

Step 1. Write a list of fifteen people who already know you can teach this. Real names. Classmates, colleagues, teachers, neighbours, group members.

Step 2. Write your specific ask in two sentences: what you teach, who for, when, how much, and what you want the person to do. Read it aloud. If it could apply to any tutor, it is not specific enough.

Step 3. Send it to five people from your list this week. Not a broadcast - five individual messages. Record who you asked and on what date.

Step 4. Record and publish one sample lesson, five to ten minutes, teaching one real thing. Use the method from lesson 2. Write down where it lives and how somebody gets to it.

Step 5. Write your proof line honestly. If you have results, name them with numbers. If you do not, write what you have genuinely done. Then read it as though you were a sceptical parent and remove anything you could not back up.

Step 6. Write your review request, word for word, and note the moment you will send it - just after a visible success. Ask for a starting point and an outcome, not for praise.

Step 7. Choose exactly two channels to be useful in for the next month: name them. For each, write the rule on advertising and what being useful there looks like in practice.

Step 8. Set your free-work limit in one line: how many free sessions, over what period, in exchange for what.

Step 9. Write your retention routine as four fixed habits you will actually do, including the written summary after each lesson and the monthly note to the parent.

Step 10. If you will teach anybody under eighteen, write your safeguarding page: how the parent consents, what you tell them about recording, what information you keep and for how long, and your rule about publishing a child's work. Add one line naming what you will confirm with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner.

quiz.question: You have no students and no reviews. What is the most effective first move?
options: Pay for social media advertising to reach strangers
Ask five specific people who already know you can teach, with a concrete description of what you offer and who it is for
Lower your rate below everyone else on the platform
Wait until your recorded course is finished

quiz.question: A parent agrees to online lessons for their 14-year-old and you want to record the sessions for revision. What is required?
options: Nothing - recording your own lesson is your business
Tell the child, since they are the student
Explain plainly who can see the recording and how long you keep it, and get the parent's written permission before recording
Record first and ask if the parent raises it
